qs.q: Which medication is noted to have adverse effects that include diarrhea, rhabdomyolysis, and polyneuropathy when used for acute gout flares?
qs.e: Colchicine can cause adverse effects such as diarrhea, rhabdomyolysis, and polyneuropathy, and is most effective when initiated within 24-36 hours of symptom onset. NSAIDs like naproxen carry different side effect profiles primarily related to the GI tract and kidneys.

ai.title: Rhabdomyolysis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rhabdomyolysis is skeletal‑muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin and CK, risking acute kidney injury. Prompt recognition, fluid resuscitation and treating the cause are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Rapid necrosis of skeletal muscle releases intracellular contents (CK, myoglobin, potassium) into the circulation. Diagnosis requires a compatible history, physical findings, and CK ≥5 000 U/L or myoglobinuria.
b: CK ≥5 000 U/L confirms significant muscle injury
Urine dipstick positive for blood with no RBCs indicates myoglobinuria

sections.p: Severity is graded by peak CK and renal function. Stages: mild (CK 5‑10 000 U/L, normal creatinine), moderate (CK 10‑50 000 U/L, rising creatinine), severe (CK >50 000 U/L, AKI, electrolyte derangement).
b: CK >50 000 U/L predicts higher risk of AKI
Serum creatinine rise >0.3 mg/dL within 48 h defines AKI

sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the common precipitants are trauma/crush, severe malaria, sickle‑cell crisis, strenuous labor, and herbal remedies containing nephrotoxins.
b: Crush injury from road traffic accidents
Severe malaria with hemolysis (black‑water fever)
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis
Intense manual labor or prolonged walking
Statin or antiretroviral toxicity
Traditional herbal concoctions (e.g., nephrotoxic roots)

sections.p: Patients report muscle pain, swelling, and weakness, often with dark‑brown urine. Systemic signs include fever, tachycardia, and oliguria if renal failure develops.
b: Muscle tenderness out of proportion to injury
Urine dark brown, dipstick + blood, no RBCs
Rapidly falling urine output

t.b: Is there significant muscle breakdown? – CK ≥5 000 U/L confirms rhabdomyolysis
Is myoglobinuria present? – Positive dipstick with absent RBCs suggests myoglobin
Is acute kidney injury or hyperkalaemia developing? – Rising creatinine or K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L signals renal compromise
Confirms myoglobin release; not essential if CK and dipstick are diagnostic
Identify infection as a trigger – Positive malaria smear guides antimalarial therapy

sections.p: Complications arise from renal tubular obstruction, electrolyte disturbances, and systemic inflammatory response.
b: Acute kidney injury (FeNa >2 % with pigmented casts)
Hyperkalaemia causing ECG changes
Metabolic acidosis
Compartment syndrome

sections.p: Early aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolytes, and removal of the inciting cause are the cornerstones.
b: IV normal saline 1‑2 L bolus, then 200‑300 mL/h to maintain urine output ≥200 mL/h
Alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate only if urine remains dark after adequate fluids and serum pH <7.35
Treat underlying cause (e.g., antimalarials, analgesia, stop offending drug)
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs)
Monitor K⁺, Ca²⁺, creatinine every 6‑12 h

sections.p: Patients need monitoring until CK falls below 5 000 U/L and renal function normalises. Education on safe labor practices and avoiding nephrotoxic herbs reduces recurrence.
b: Re‑check CK and creatinine at 48‑72 h
Counsel on gradual increase in physical activity
Screen for sickle‑cell disease or HIV if recurrent

sections.p: Conditions that also cause dark urine and muscle pain can be mistaken for rhabdomyolysis.
b: Hematuria from urinary tract infection – dipstick shows blood with RBCs
Acute hemolysis (e.g., black‑water fever) – urine dipstick positive for blood with RBCs and low haptoglobin

sections.p: Certain laboratory findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Serum CK may be normal early (<6 h) – repeat if suspicion persists
Urine dipstick can be false‑negative if myoglobin is diluted

whenToSeekHelp: Serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L or ECG changes

faq.q: Why is CK preferred over myoglobin for diagnosis?
faq.a: CK remains elevated for days, while myoglobin clears quickly and is less specific.

faq.q: Can normal urine dipstick rule out rhabdomyolysis?
faq.a: No; early or dilute urine may miss myoglobin, so CK is essential.
Only if urine stays dark despite adequate fluids or if severe acidosis is present.

exam: What immediate step do you take for a patient with crush injury and dark urine? — Start rapid isotonic fluid bolus to protect kidneys.
How do you differentiate myoglobinuria from hematuria on a dipstick? — Myoglobinuria shows +blood with no RBCs on microscopy.
Which electrolyte abnormality is most life‑threatening in rhabdomyolysis and how do you monitor it? — Hyperkalaemia; check serum K⁺ and ECG every 6 h.
What are the key indications for adding sodium bicarbonate to fluids? — Persistent dark urine after adequate fluids or serum pH <7.35.
Why must nephrotoxic drugs be stopped even if they treat a co‑existing condition? — They worsen tubular injury and increase AKI risk.
In a low‑resource setting without CK assay, what clinical clues guide diagnosis? — Severe muscle pain, swelling, dark urine, recent trauma or malaria, and rising creatinine.
What complication should prompt urgent surgical consultation? — Compartment syndrome with tense swelling and pain on passive stretch.
How does severe malaria precipitate rhabdomyolysis? — Parasite‑induced hemolysis and microvascular obstruction cause muscle ischemia and myoglobin release.
